When checked, the nuclides decay during the measurement will be accounted for, with the quoted relative activity being the activity at the start of measurement.

When checked, this nuclides mass-fraction uncertainty is computed with a profile-likelihood scan - the problem is re-solved with the fraction fixed at trial values, and the 68.3% and 95.4% confidence intervals read from where the chi-squared rises by the corresponding amount. This gives an asymmetric interval that stays valid near the physical 0% and 100% bounds (where the standard covariance-based uncertainty is unreliable), at the cost of some extra computation time. Results appear in the chart title and below the mass-fraction table.

The functional form to use for the relative efficiency curve.
Options are:
Log(energy): y = a + b*ln(x) + c*(ln(x))^2 + d*(ln(x))^3 + ...
Log(rel. eff.): y = exp( a + b*x + c/x + d/x^2 + e/x^3 + ... )
Log(energy)Log(rel. eff.): y = exp( a + b*(lnx) + c*(lnx)^2 + d*(lnx)^3 + ... )
FRAM Empirical: y = exp( a + b/x^2 + c*(lnx) + d*(lnx)^2 + e*(lnx)^3 )
FRAM Physical: y =
(1 - exp(-AD0*μ0))
(AD0*μ0)
* [exp(-AD1*μ1) * exp(-AD2*μ2) + ...] * [Det. Eff.] * [Eb * C1/E]
The order (how many energy-dependent terms) relative efficiency equation to use.
When checked, the Modified Hoerl correction factor (i.e. Eb * C1/E) is used to account for differences between the physical model and/or detector efficiency, and observed data.
The nuclear data source for gamma branching ratios.

The number of FWHM, from the peak mean, to include source gammas from as contributing to a peaks area.
For some photopeaks of some nuclides multiple gammas that are close in energy may contribute to creating a detected peak area. This match tolerance specifies how many FWHM from the observed peak mean source gammas should be summed to determine the branching ratio to use.
Specifying a value of zero will will cause only the gamma energy assigned to a peak to be used, even if there are very nearby other gammas.

How each peak is weighted in the relative efficiency fit, and how the resulting uncertainties are reported.
Stat. Only (default) weights each peak by its own counting statistics. If the peaks then scatter about the fitted curve by more than those uncertainties allow - which is usual, since the efficiency model is never perfect - the reported uncertainties are widened to match the scatter actually seen. The widening ignores a few badly mis-fit peaks, so one bad peak does not inflate everything.
Auto does the same thing, but applies the widening to each peak's uncertainty up front rather than to the final answer, so you can see it in the chart's error bars. Since every peak is scaled by the same factor, the fitted values are identical to Stat. Only - only the uncertainties differ in how they are presented.
Stat. Only (no widening) reports the purely statistical uncertainty, as if the efficiency model were exactly right. On real spectra this is usually much too small; use it only when you specifically want the statistical figure.
1% through 100% add a fixed uncertainty in proportion to each peak's area. Be aware this changes how the peaks are weighted relative to each other - it takes influence away from the high-statistics peaks - and against certified uranium reference materials it was found to shift the fitted enrichment downward (by around 0.2 to 2 percentage points, growing with the percentage and levelling off around 25%). They are kept for compatibility and for cases where you want to force the curve to pass more evenly through all the points.
Unweighted lets every peak contribute equally, no matter its statistical uncertainty.
